name: David Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, David. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. What you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior doctor at Market Square Medical, a privately run clinic in a busy town centre, where a lot of patients pay a monthly membership on top of the public appointments. I see about twenty-four people a day: back pain, anxiety, children's ear infections, the odd business owner who wants a full check-up in fifteen minutes. I use AI all day, for notes, for checking drug doses, and for drafting letters, and I'm usually the first to try anything new the clinic buys.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pace, and I like that the owners actually listen when I suggest something. What wears me out is knowing I'm still behind the experienced doctors on judgement, and no software fixes that yet. Outside work I coach the under-twelves rugby team on Saturdays, which keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that would be a bit disappointing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype got ahead of the product, which happens with every new technology. I'd still say the useful tools are worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. The clinic is busy, the owners are doing well, and my pay is normal for a junior. I'd just have to get better the slow way, by seeing a lot of patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I have and keep putting two hundred a month into a share fund, on top of my savings of about four months. I'd sit my family medicine exams next spring. And I'd keep sketching out the plan for my own small clinic one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, like a match that ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own clinic? Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small practice in the new housing estate on the edge of town, where families are moving in and there's no doctor yet. Low rent, good software, two doctors and a nurse. It's ten years off, but I think about it on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about money that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I don't have a car loan, I rent a small flat, and I've got no one depending on me yet. My main worry is that I'm not a good enough doctor yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for patients and for clinics willing to change. I'd tell colleagues the clinics that adopt early will win, and the slow ones will struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. The owners like that I set up the tools, and that makes me harder to let go. The risk is that fewer junior doctors get hired overall, but I'd rather be the junior who runs the software than one who's replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to lead the clinic's AI rollout and ask for a small pay rise for doing it, maybe next year. I'd take an online course in running a medical practice, the business side. And I'd keep investing a bit each month in companies building these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I'd feel ahead of the game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gwen on reception, who's been there twenty years and hates computers. I'd sit with her and show her the booking system before the owners get any ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any downside you'd admit to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that I learn less if the machine does the thinking for me. I'd have to force myself to work things out first, then check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a sprint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should let it run but make sure doctors stay legally responsible, so patients have someone to hold to account. I'd argue against heavy rules that just protect big hospitals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. My edge is being good with tools, and if the tool is better than every doctor, my edge is gone. The thinking part of my job goes in 2028, and the hands-on part, like examining and injecting, goes when robots come in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring forward my own clinic plan by years: a small practice where one doctor supervises AI and does the hands-on work, started in 2027 with a bank loan and help from my parents. I'd sell some of my shares to fund it. And I'd learn every procedure I can before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a lot of energy. A bit like kick-off in a final.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A bank loan in that world? Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. But waiting is risky too. If I'm going to lose the job anyway, I'd rather lose it running my own place than waiting for a letter from the owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say go for it, he started his own building firm at twenty-six. My mum would ask whether I'm eating properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more my speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this gives business time to adapt, and governments should mostly stay out of the way. I'd post about it on a doctors' forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well. Five years is time to qualify, learn the business side, and open my own practice before 2031. The hands-on work runs to around 2034, which gives the practice a few good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify first, then open the practice on the new housing estate in 2029. I'd keep investing a bit in health tech shares. And I'd take a course in minor surgery so the practice can offer more than a screen can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practice look like by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably one doctor, a nurse, and a lot of software. Maybe by then the robots do the bloods. I'd adapt again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the under-twelves you coach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the under-twelves to learn a skill and how to run a business. Being employed by someone else is the riskiest job there is now.

I'd say governments should mostly **stay out** of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's my plan, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and we should let the market sort out the details. I'd say young doctors should learn business and tools, not wait for a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be very comfortable. My own practice would have years to grow before 2036, and the hands-on work goes on to around 2039. By then I'd hopefully have a family and an established business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the practice around 2030, as I always pictured. I'd keep investing every month and add a small share of a physiotherapy business in town. And I'd probably get married and settle, because there'd be time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a long season with a clear plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would knock you off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big chain buying up every small practice with AI before I'm ready. I'd watch for that and move earlier if I saw it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What role would faith play in this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Church keeps me grounded. Whatever the machines do, I'd want my kids to know work and community matter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to bet everything on a practice before I'm even qualified. What would help is fast licences for small new practices, and lighter rules for doctors who supervise AI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'm scared. I am, a little, in the fast one. I just think the best cure for fear is building something.

headlineQuote: The best cure for fear is building something.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior doctor at a privately run town-centre clinic who uses **AI daily**.
He coaches **youth rugby**, goes to church and already invests monthly in shares.
He's **calm** in slower pictures and expects to gain from steady change.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious**, and he'd respond by opening his **own practice** early.
He wants **light regulation** and leans on family, not government.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have to bet everything before qualifying.
whatWouldHelp: **Lighter rules** for doctors who supervise AI.
